title: Billing for Microsoft Fabric Planning (Preview)
summary: Microsoft explains the billing model behind Planning in Microsoft Fabric (Preview), an enterprise-planning experience built on Fabric IQ, describing why it uses a hybrid role/session-based pricing structure for people plus job-based pricing for automation rather than pure consumption or seat licensing, and how that usage surfaces in the Capacity Metrics app.
audience: Fabric capacity owners, FinOps/IT admins, and planning/FP&A stakeholders who need to forecast and monitor capacity-unit spend before Planning reaches general availability.
why_it_matters: Enterprise planning workloads are cyclical and bursty rather than steady, so a capacity owner who assumes standard Fabric consumption-pricing intuition will misjudge Planning cost; understanding the session and job billing units matters before GA billing starts.
takeaways: Planning in Microsoft Fabric uses a hybrid pricing model rather than pure consumption or flat seat licensing, because planning usage is cyclical and bursty rather than continuous.
People-based usage is billed through role-scoped, time-bound sessions, while automated data sync/refresh work is billed per successful job.
All Planning usage draws from the workspace's existing Fabric capacity units (CUs) rather than a separate subscription or license.
During the preview, Capacity Metrics shows Planning consumption but does not yet charge for it; charging begins at general availability.
Fabric Planning is called out as scheduled to reach general availability in July 2026, per this post.

claims.text: Planning in Microsoft Fabric (Preview) unifies planning, analytics, reporting, and data management into a single Fabric experience rather than a separate standalone tool.

Microsoft designed Planning's billing model around the observation that enterprise planning workloads are cyclical, with concentrated high-intensity usage at month-end and quarter/year-end forecasting, unlike the steady, incremental usage pattern of most analytics workloads.

Microsoft states that pure consumption pricing would undervalue Planning because its critical work happens in short bursts, and that flat seat-based licensing feels rigid because it charges for users who only participate occasionally.
Fabric Planning bills people-facing usage through role- and session-based pricing, and bills automated operations like data sync and sheet updates through per-successful-job pricing.

Planning defines three user roles with different pricing weight: Viewers (read-only, priced low to encourage adoption), Stakeholders (active participants, priced for engagement), and Planners (model owners running scenarios, priced for their outsized impact on decisions).

A Planning session binds a user, their role, a specific Fabric capacity, and a time window; a session starts when a user meaningfully engages with a planning artifact and then runs for a fixed 30-day (730-hour) period.
The fixed 30-day session window is intended to smooth cost over time so that a short burst of planning activity is not penalized as if it were continuous heavy usage.
All Fabric Planning usage, for both user sessions and automation jobs, is metered against the workspace's existing Fabric capacity units and requires no separate subscription or license.
Because Planning shares the same Fabric capacity pool as other workloads, capacity left unused by Planning can be consumed by other Fabric workloads on the same capacity, and vice versa.

Planning consumption is visible in the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app by filtering to Experience = Planning, which surfaces Planner/Viewer session activity, automation job counts, and the CUs each consumes.
During the Planning preview, Capacity Metrics shows usage only, with no dollar charges applied; billing for Planning is stated to begin at general availability.
The post states that Fabric Planning is scheduled to reach general availability in July 2026.
